report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Executive summary

On 07/07/2026 MV Tarrakin Star, a 24.4 m aluminium catamaran passenger ferry certificated for 96 passengers, grounded on Boolarong Bank in the Merrandi Channel at 18:12:04 while inbound on service TF18, at 6.8 kt over the ground, on a falling tide in darkness. All times in this report are local time (UTC+10). The vessel came to rest 74 m west of the charted centreline and 54 m outside the dredged channel, heeled 4 degrees to starboard, with 38 passengers, a master, a deckhand and a kiosk attendant on board. There were no serious injuries. One passenger reported a grazed shin and two were treated at the wharf for distress. All passengers were ashore by 19:26. The vessel suffered substantial damage, including a 180 mm split in the starboard hull plating in way of the No. 2 void, with flooding of that void to about 260 mm by the time it refloated at 00:20 on 08/07/2026. The Merrandi Channel was closed to commercial traffic for 19 hours.

The Investigation found that a series of organisational gaps left the Master without a defence when the chart plotter failed. The last service was moved into darkness from 01/06/2026 without reopening the route risk assessment that restricted the channel to "daylight transits only", so no night passage plan or hold point existed for the loss of the primary position fix. It is likely that the unreopened assessment led to that absence, and very likely that the absence allowed the transit to continue at eight knots after the plotter froze at 18:07:06. The operator's defect procedure never required a fault that had cleared itself to be recorded, so earlier freezes were never written down and the manufacturer's firmware fix, issued in 11/2024, was never applied. It is likely that this led to the freeze.

The heading then eased from 195 to 200 degrees without a decision to turn, and the vessel left the channel on the bank side. The No. 4 beacon, the one reference left, was screened by mangroves from 0.84 to 0.34 nm. It is very likely that the Port Authority's deferral of the clearing work, unfunded at three works rounds, led to that screening, and likely that the screening let the heading go unnoticed. The shallow alarm was still at its 2019 setting of 0.9 m and gave 16 seconds' warning against a 92 m crash stop. It is extremely likely that this limited the margin to contact.

After the grounding the Master stopped both engines within 27 seconds, decided not to refloat, broadcast a pan pan at 18:13:04 and addressed the passengers within 36 seconds. This very likely reduced risk, because the vessel was holed in the compartment it rested on.

Other factors increased risk without influencing this occurrence: the aids code set no notice or availability duty for beacons off declared channels, the beacon's range was halved by a solar conversion without notice to channel users, the roster placed the darkness transit at the end of a split duty, and a plotter fault was passed on verbally and not entered in the defect book. The lifejacket locker arrangement in the forward saloon is still being examined. Whether unshielded floodlights behind the beacon delayed its sighting, and whether the Master was fatigued, could not be settled and no finding is made on either.

Work order WO-176 was funded and the canopy trimmed to 2 m on 24/07/2026. Local notice LNM-2026-14 was issued on 22/07/2026, and the passage plan was reissued as issue 3 with the corrected range. Two recommendations remain open, with responses due 30/09/2026: a sightline test in place of the 50 m vegetation scope in the services agreement, and a night passage plan naming a hold point for the loss of the primary fix.

Event overview

This section describes the occurrence in the order it happened, from the vessel and the conditions, through the channel transit and the grounding, to the response and the damage.

Vessel, operator and crew

MV Tarrakin Star is a 24.4 m aluminium catamaran passenger ferry certificated for 96 passengers, operated by Tarrakin Ferries on the Muntari Island route to Kanooka Heads. On 07/07/2026 the vessel was on service TF18, the last return service of the day. It carried 38 passengers, a master, a deckhand and a kiosk attendant.

The Master held a master's certificate for sheltered-waters passenger vessels, held since 2012. The Master had 14 years as a master, 11 of them with Tarrakin Ferries on this route, and had made approximately 4,100 transits of the Merrandi Channel. The last route check was on 14/02/2026 and was satisfactory. The Deckhand had been with the operator for 7 months and held a basic marine safety certificate and a coxswain's certificate. The outgoing master, who worked the morning shift, had 9 years as a master, 4 of them on this route, and approximately 1,400 transits of the channel.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: vessel registration, build details beyond the 2011 approved arrangement, and the regulatory status of the operator]

Conditions and the channel

Sunset was at 17:02 and civil twilight ended at 17:29. Moonrise was at 06:12 with the moon 2% illuminated, so the transit was made in full darkness. At 18:00 the wind was from 305 degrees at 8 kt, visibility was more than 10 km and rainfall since 09:00 was nil. The port workboat reported a slight sea at 18:45, with wind ripple only and no swell penetrating the entrance. The tide was falling. The Port Authority gauge at Kanooka Heads read 0.91 m at 18:12, against a predicted 0.94 m.

The Merrandi Channel is 40 m wide, dredged to 3.2 m, and marked by six beacons. It is not a declared shipping channel. Boolarong Bank lies to its west and dries in places. The passage plan gave the transit speed as 8 knots on a course of 195 degrees true inbound.

Before the voyage

The Master took over the vessel from the outgoing master at the town wharf at about 13:05. The plotter's event log records two freezes on the morning shift, at 10:42 and 11:17, both with cause code 0x51, and the unit recovered itself each time. According to both masters, the outgoing master told the Master about both freezes at the handover, and the Master replied that the plotter had done the same a month earlier. Neither made an entry in the wheelhouse defect book, and no entry of any kind was made for 07/07/2026 before the occurrence.

The voyage and the channel transit

TF18 departed Muntari Island at 17:35:02 and reported its departure to Port Control on VHF channel 12 with 38 passengers. This was the thirty-first darkness transit of the channel since the winter timetable began on 01/06/2026.

The vessel entered the Merrandi Channel from the north at 18:03:58, abeam the No. 1 beacon, 2 m east of the charted centreline at 8.4 kt on a course of 195 degrees. At 18:04:14 the Deckhand left the bridge to collect fares after the Master said, "Nah, go and do the fares, I'll give you a yell coming up on the wharf." At 18:05:30 the vessel was abeam the No. 2 beacon, 1 m west of the centreline, 0.90 nm north of the No. 4 beacon.

At 18:07:06 the plotter's event log recorded the display process not responding, with no reset. The Master's account was that the chart picture stayed on the screen with the vessel symbol stationary and no response to touch. The bridge audio has "Oh, come on" at 18:07:11, sounds consistent with repeated screen taps at 18:07:26 and "(unintelligible) frozen again" at 18:07:44. The vessel was then 3 m west of the centreline at 8.4 kt, on a course of 196 degrees, 0.68 nm north of the No. 4 beacon.

From that second the heading increased steadily from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute and was then held. The recorded rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute at 18:07:40 and returned to zero by 18:08:50. The Master said in interview that the vessel was eased to starboard while the Master was at the plotter and then looking for the beacon, and that the Master never made a decision to turn. No throttle movement was recorded, and speed was 8.1 kt at 18:08:00.

At 18:08:31 the Master said, "Right. Where's four." The vessel was then 12 m west of the centreline and 0.47 nm north of the No. 4 beacon. At about 18:09:00 the vessel reached the channel's western edge, 20 m west of the centreline at 0.40 nm, with the course over the ground at 199 degrees and speed 8.0 kt. A sound consistent with a window or door being slid open was recorded at 18:09:40. The Master said the window was opened in case the glass was the problem.

At 18:10:02 the Master said, "There's four. Bring her back." The vessel was then 39 m west of the centreline, 0.25 nm north of the beacon, on a course of 200 degrees at 7.9 kt, outside the dredged channel. The Master said the beacon was dead ahead rather than on the starboard bow, and that the Master knew then of being off the line to the west. The Master brought the vessel back to port, believing it to be just outside the edge, when it was nearly 40 m out. The course over the ground eased from 200 to 197 degrees but stayed west of the channel's 195 degrees. At 18:11:00 the vessel was 58 m west of the centreline, over Boolarong Bank, at 7.6 kt.

The echo sounder's shallow alarm sounded at 18:11:48, with the vessel 70 m west of the centreline at 7.1 kt. The bridge audio has "No no no" at 18:11:50. Both throttles were moved astern together at 18:11:52. Contact with Boolarong Bank followed at 18:12:04 at 6.8 kt over the ground, 16 seconds after the alarm. The audio recorded a heavy impact and about 9 seconds of grinding and vibration. The vessel stopped within 11 m and came to rest 74 m west of the charted centreline, 54 m outside the dredged channel, heeled 4 degrees to starboard, on a falling tide. Both engines were stopped at 18:12:31 and were not restarted.

The response

At 18:12:40 the Master addressed the passengers, and the kiosk attendant was heard asking whether everyone was all right. At 18:13:04 the Master broadcast a pan pan on VHF channel 16, giving the position, the 38 passengers and 3 crew, no injuries reported and no pollution, and stating "I am not attempting to refloat." Port Control acknowledged at 18:13:29 and called the workboat. The Master addressed the passengers again at 18:14:52 and told them lifejackets were being handed out.

The Deckhand reported water in the No. 2 void at 18:16:20, two or three inches on the sounding rod. At 18:17:05 the Master reported to Port Control approximately 75 mm of ingress into the No. 2 starboard void, to be monitored ten minutely. The Deckhand reported at 18:22:40 that everyone was in a jacket, and that two passengers in the forward saloon had required the Deckhand to go round the servery because the locker was behind the counter. The Deckhand's report, which is protected, also describes issuing jackets in the forward saloon past three people standing at the counter. The arrangement of that locker is still being examined.

The port workboat came alongside at 18:41. The last passenger was ashore at 19:26, and the crew of three remained on board. The vessel refloated on the rising tide at 00:20 on 08/07/2026 and was towed to the town wharf, where a starboard hull breach and progressive flooding of the No. 2 void were confirmed. The Merrandi Channel was closed to commercial traffic for 19 hours.

Damage and injuries

The survey found the starboard hull bottom plating set up over 4.1 m between frames 6 and 11, with a 180 mm split in way of the No. 2 void. Ingress reached approximately 260 mm by the time the vessel refloated. All three blades of the starboard propeller were bent aft, the shaft was bent 1.4 mm, the starboard rudder stock was distorted 3 degrees, and the starboard skeg was torn away. The port hull, propulsion and steering had no damage.

There were no serious injuries. One passenger reported a grazed shin, and two passengers were treated at the wharf for distress.

Personnel accounts

Three interviews were held. The Master and the outgoing master, who worked the morning shift, were interviewed and their records are finalised. A third interview was held with the Deckhand, but its record is not finalised and its content is not reported here. The Master and the Deckhand each submitted a safety report under a confidential scheme, and these are attributed by role and not quoted.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the kiosk attendant's role in the response, account and any statement, since no interview or report from that person is held]

Analysis

This analysis follows the occurrence in the order it developed: the operator's planning documents, the loss of the plotter and the absence of any hold point, the heading change and the screened beacon, and the final seconds before contact. It then deals with the factors that increased risk without influencing this occurrence, the two matters that could not be settled, the hypotheses not supported, and what worked.

The transit as planned and what the operator's documents required

OPS-3 3.4 required that "The Merrandi Channel transit will be made on the charted centreline, monitored on the chart plotter, with the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons identified visually before the vessel passes the No. 1 beacon." OPS-3 3.2 required the master to "conduct the passage in accordance with the plan" and to record any departure in the deck log. Appendix A, issue 2 and current, named the chart plotter as the primary means of position fixing and the visual transit of the No. 4 beacon with the town wharf leading lights as the secondary. It stated: "this plan is written for the daylight transit. Night transits are not scheduled on this route."

RRA-07 issue 2 carried the same restriction, "daylight transits only", and added that "A night transit of the Merrandi Channel requires the General Manager Operations' approval and a specific passage plan." It named a single unlit reach between the No. 2 and No. 4 beacons as a hazard.

CHG-2026-014 moved service TF18 from 16:15 to 17:35 from 01/06/2026 to meet a coach connection. It assessed the change as "timetable change only", recorded "No new hazard identified", and answered "No" to route risk assessment review. The Operations Manager approved it on 22/04/2026, one level below the General Manager Operations. The restriction in RRA-07 was not referenced, RRA-07 was not reopened and no issue 3 exists. No night passage plan was written, and the General Manager Operations' approval was neither sought nor given.

From 01/06/2026 the transit was made after the end of civil twilight at 17:29 on every day the service ran. TF18 ran 31 times in darkness, and the occurrence was the thirty-first. The Master made 26 of the 30 earlier darkness transits and the outgoing master, morning shift, made the other four. The Master said that the change reached the crew as a new roster sheet, with no brief, plan or conversation. The Operations Manager's understanding of the restriction was given verbally. [NOT ESTABLISHED: why the change was assessed as a timetable change only] [NOT ESTABLISHED: the Operations Manager's formal account of what the restriction was understood to require]

A reopened assessment might have produced a night plan that said no more than the daylight one, with no hold point, and the vessel would then have met the frozen plotter in the same way. That possibility goes to how good the plan would have been, not to whether one would have existed. RRA-07 named both the plan and the approver, so a review that read it could not have closed without a plan. A plan written for this channel is also the document most likely to say what to do when the primary fix is lost. Both the freeze and the departure from the channel occurred in the unlit reach that RRA-07 itself identified. It is therefore likely that the failure to reopen the daylight-only assessment led to there being no night passage plan and no hold point for the loss of the primary fix. The Investigation found that the last service was moved into darkness without the assessment being reopened.

No plan or hold point for the loss of the primary fix

The operator had no night passage plan for the Merrandi Channel and no guidance anywhere on what to do if the plotter was lost during the transit. The plan named no abort or hold point. OPS-3 3.6 required a reduction of speed, and consideration of anchoring or returning to open water, but only "In reduced visibility". Visibility on the night was more than 10 km, so that provision did not apply. The secondary means in Appendix A did not cover the gap either. The leading lights lay about 1.9 nm beyond the No. 6 beacon and did not resolve as two lights until the vessel was inside the channel's southern third. At the point where the plotter was lost, the No. 4 beacon was therefore the whole of the secondary means.

Both masters interviewed gave the same account of what stopping would have meant. The outgoing master, morning shift, said that had the plotter frozen inside the channel the right course would have been to take the way off the vessel and wait until it recovered or the marks confirmed the position, because there was no traffic and nothing to hit while stopped. This master knew of no rule requiring it. The Master said that, when the plotter froze, they did not consider stopping and went straight to the visual transit because in their mind it was the backup. In the Master's words: "There's nothing that tells you to stop. There's nothing that tells you anything."

The conditions favoured a stop. There was no other traffic, the water was flat and the wind was offshore at 8 kt. The vessel's trials figure for a crash stop from 8 kt was 92 m. The AIS track showed 8.4 kt at the freeze at 18:07:06 and 8.1 kt at 18:08:00. The later fall to 7.1 kt by 18:11:48 matched shoaling drag, with no throttle movement until 18:11:52. The vessel crossed the channel's western edge about 114 seconds after the freeze. A stop begun at any point in that time would have left it in the channel, and a stop begun before about 18:11:40 would still have halted it short of the contact point. That included the 98 seconds after the Master saw the beacon dead ahead at 18:10:02 and knew of being off the line. A stop after the sighting would have left the vessel on the bank's margin, upright and not holed.

No lookout was on the bridge from 18:04:14, when the Deckhand was sent to collect fares. This was the normal practice on the route and OPS-3 did not address it either way.

A master who had not thought of stopping unprompted might not have applied a written rule under the same pressure, and this was the reservation against the factor. It did not carry, because a named hold point would have applied throughout the 114 seconds, and both masters independently identified stopping as the correct response. The absence of any hold point very likely allowed the transit to continue at eight knots after the freeze. It is extremely likely that continuing with no means of fixing the vessel's position allowed it to leave the channel on the bank side, and this left the shallow alarm as the only remaining defence. The Investigation found that the operator's defence against this sequence was never written.

The plotter freeze and the defect chain

The plotter's own event log recorded cause code 0x51 at 10:42 and 11:17 on the morning of 07/07/2026, with the unit recovering itself each time. At 18:07:06 it recorded the display process not responding, with no reset. The bridge audio matched this. The Master said "Oh, come on" at 18:07:11, repeated screen taps were audible at 18:07:26, and at 18:07:44 the Master said "(unintelligible) frozen again". The Master described the chart picture staying on the screen with the vessel symbol stationary and no response to touch. A 46 hour bench test on 21/07/2026, with the same antenna and cabling, did not reproduce the fault and found no defect. The contractor identified cause code 0x51 as known to the manufacturer and addressed by firmware issued in 11/2024, which had not been applied to this unit. The unit ran firmware issued 03/2024.

From the freeze the Master had no position fix of any kind, and the search for the beacon began 85 seconds later. The heading began to ease in the same second as the freeze. It is extremely likely that the freeze led both to the heading change and to the continuation of the transit at eight knots.

The fault had been seen before and none of those events was recorded. OPS-9 9.1 required immediate reporting and an entry in the defect book only for a defect that rendered the vessel unseaworthy or affected a statutory item. The plotter was not a statutory item on this vessel on this route, although it was the primary means of position fixing. OPS-9 9.2 required all other defects to be entered "at the end of the shift in which they are found", for weekly review by the Operations Manager. For a fault that had come and gone, that gave no trigger at all, and the manual did not say whether such a fault was a defect. OPS-9 9.3 required the outgoing master to brief the relieving master on "any defect" but required nothing to be written down.

The book carried eleven entries in the 90 days before the occurrence, all for faults present when written, and none concerned the plotter. The maintenance system held no work order, fault report or correspondence about the plotter in 2026. The operator held no subscription to the manufacturer's bulletins. The outgoing master said that the plotter had frozen three or four times on this vessel in the previous year without being written up, and the Master said it had frozen a month earlier. Both described the same reading of the book, which the Master put as: "The book is for things that are broken when you hand over. If it's broken you write it, if it came good you say it."

Recorded freezes would have reached the Operations Manager's weekly review and the maintenance system, and from there the contractor, who identified the code in one bench test. The chain from an entry to an applied fix still ran through someone ashore finding the manufacturer's bulletin, which the operator did not receive. A recorded freeze might therefore have been reviewed, noted and left, and nothing shows how many entries it would have taken, or how quickly. A year of freezes on the vessel's primary means of fixing going to nobody still meant that no freeze was ever on paper, so the fix was never applied. It is likely that the absence of any requirement to record a self-cleared fault led to the plotter freeze occurring at 18:07. Both masters volunteered the omission before they were asked about it. The Master identified the Master's own part in it without prompting. The Investigation found that the defect procedure gave no trigger for recording a fault that had cleared itself.

The heading change and the screened beacon

From 18:07:06 the heading increased steadily from 195 to 200 degrees over about a minute and was then held. The rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute at 18:07:40, while the Master was at the frozen screen, and returned to zero by 18:08:50. Rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees throughout, so the turn was steered. The wind was offshore at 8 kt and there was no cross-set at that state of tide. The held heading set the vessel west at about 20 m a minute, and it reached the 20 m western edge at about 18:09:00. The Master's own account was: "I eased her to starboard while I was fiddling with the plotter and then looking for four. Five degrees. I never made that decision." Nothing on the bridge showed the new heading to the Master, because the plotter symbol was frozen and the beacon was not visible. The heading change was the action that took the vessel out of the channel.

The beacon could have shown the Master the new heading, and it was screened. The range and visibility check of 18/07/2026 was made from the port workboat on the inbound track at the same time of night. It found the No. 4 beacon not visible from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it, because the sightline passed through the mangrove canopy on Merrandi Islet, about 240 m up-channel of the beacon. The canopy measured 5.8 m against a lantern height of 4.2 m. The Master began the search at 18:08:31 with "Right. Where's four", when the vessel was 0.47 nm north of the beacon. The Master slid the wheelhouse window open at 18:09:40 and called "There's four. Bring her back" at 18:10:02, at 0.25 nm. The vessel crossed the western edge at about 0.40 nm, inside the screened arc. Seen on the starboard bow, where it belongs, the light would have shown the vessel drawing west within a minute of the turn, while it was still in the channel.

The heading change began before the search, so the screening explains why the turn went unnoticed and not why it began. The light was also clear of the islet for at least the last 37 seconds of the search, from about 18:09:25, and was not seen in that time. Those seconds are the subject of the floodlight matter below and do not undo the screening that preceded them. It is likely that the screening allowed the held heading to go unnoticed over the minute and a half in which it mattered.

The Authority's own register shows how the screening arose. The 2019 aerial survey gave the canopy at 2.1 m, so it grew about half a metre a year. Work order WO-118, raised in 09/2023, recommended trimming to 2 m on a three-yearly cycle at an estimated $18,500. It was deferred as unfunded at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds, and WO-176 in 03/2026 recorded the sightline as fully closed on the northern approach. The Authority's file note against WO-176 said the islet was 240 m from the beacon and so outside the 50 m scope of schedule 2.4 of the services agreement. That schedule provided: "Vegetation management within 50 m of an aid is a works item and is funded from the general waterways maintenance vote. Vegetation beyond 50 m is not within the scope of this agreement." The work therefore competed with boat ramps and pontoons in the general waterways vote.

The monthly check required by schedule 2.1 was made from the town wharf, 2.1 nm south of the beacon, from which the islet is not in the line of sight. The register therefore recorded the beacon as observed and operating every month from 01/2024 to 07/2026, and no defect was ever recorded against it. A trim funded at the 2023 round would have left the canopy near 3.5 m on the night, under the lantern. The growth may not have been even across the seven years, because only two measurements, in 2019 and 2026, were taken. It is very likely that the deferral of the clearing, three times and unfunded, led to the beacon being screened over the stretch where the vessel left the channel. Neither the masters' reports to each other nor the company's reporting system reached the Authority, and the Master said there was nowhere to put them. The Investigation found that the beacon was screened from the channel over the stretch where it was needed, and that the clearing had been deferred for three works rounds.

Leaving the channel and the final seconds

The AIS track showed the vessel 1 m west of the centreline abeam the No. 2 beacon at 18:05:30 and 3 m west at the freeze. It was 7 m west at 18:08:00, 12 m west at 18:08:31 and 20 m west at 18:09:00. It was 39 m west at 18:10:02, 58 m west at 18:11:00 and 70 m west at 18:11:48. The channel was 40 m wide and dredged to 3.2 m, and the bank on its western side dries in places and shoals at about 1 in 70. The vessel was over the bank from about 18:11:00. The grounding followed directly and only from the vessel being outside the dredged channel.

When the Master saw the beacon dead ahead at 18:10:02, the Master brought the vessel back to port, believing the vessel to be just outside the edge, a boat width perhaps, when it was 39 m west of the centreline. In the Master's words, stopping "on the edge of a bank I couldn't see, felt worse than easing her back in". The course over ground came back from 200 to 197 degrees, a turn of about three degrees to port. That slowed the westing but kept the course west of the channel's 195 degrees to the contact.

The echo sounder's shallow alarm was set to 0.9 m under the keel, the value entered at commissioning in 2019 and never changed. It sounded once, at 18:11:48. Both throttles went astern together four seconds later and contact followed at 18:12:04, 16 seconds after the alarm, at 6.8 kt. At 7.1 kt the vessel covered 58 m in that time against a trials crash stop figure of 92 m. Astern thrust was developing but had not reached full at contact. On the surveyed 1 in 70 gradient the alarm could not have sounded appreciably earlier at that setting.

A setting of about 1.6 m under the keel would have sounded about 107 m short of the contact, enough for a crash stop with four seconds to react. It would still not have sounded in the dredged channel at low water, so the setting has to be chosen for the channel and not simply raised. The equipment did exactly what it was set to do. It is extremely likely that the 2019 setting limited the warning to 16 seconds and so led to the grounding. The vessel stopped within 11 m and heeled 4 degrees to starboard. The bed at the contact point was 0.50 m below chart datum, and 30 m further west it was 0.35 m higher, where the vessel would have taken the ground harder and listed more. The Investigation found that the vessel left the dredged channel on the bank side and that the alarm gave less warning than the vessel needed to stop.

Factors that increased risk but did not influence this occurrence

The following factors existed and increased risk. None of them changed the course of this occurrence.

The aids code set no notice or availability duty for the beacons on this channel. WAN-2 4.2 applied an availability target of 99.0 per cent, a duty to record availability, and a duty to notify a change to an aid's character, position or range "by notice to mariners before the change takes effect", but only for an aid on a declared shipping channel. The Merrandi Channel is not one, so 4.3 applied instead and required only that the authority "be able to demonstrate that the aid is inspected at intervals it has determined and recorded". WAN-2 4.1, which required every aid to be maintained so that it "performs the function for which it was established", has no channel threshold and applied throughout. Had 4.2 applied, a range change would have gone out as a notice and availability would have been recorded. Neither mechanism reaches this occurrence. A notice would have told the operator about a light that was screened where the vessel left the channel, and a better known light is no more visible through a canopy. An availability figure measures whether a light is lit, and this one was lit throughout. The screening was kept in place by the 50 m scope of the services agreement and not by the code. It is unlikely that the code's thresholds influenced the occurrence. It is likely that they increased risk, because the operator of a 96-passenger ferry in darkness has no right to be told of a change to a beacon.

The solar conversion of the No. 4 beacon in 11/2025 reduced its nominal range from 6 nm to 3 nm, with the character Fl G 2.5s unchanged. The hydrographic service was notified on 04/02/2026 and the chart correction was still pending on 07/07/2026. No local notice was issued, no operator was told, and the operator's passage plan appendix still gave the beacon at 6 M. The measurement on 18/07/2026 gave a luminous range of 2.6 nm. The Master already knew the light was weaker, saying "It used to be a proper light. It was a mains light." The search ran from 0.47 nm to 0.25 nm, well inside even the measured range. Over most of that distance the canopy screened the light, and a screened light is not made visible by being brighter. It is unlikely that the conversion influenced the occurrence. It is likely that it increased risk, because a master working to the plan on a night when the light is not screened would be looking for something twice as strong as what is there.

The roster put the last darkness transit of the day at the end of a split duty, 05:40 to 08:40 and 13:00 to 19:20, on every day of a 12 days on, 2 days off tour. That was 9 hours 20 minutes of duty across a 13 hour 40 minute spread, against the operator's limits of 10 hours and 14 hours. On 07/07/2026 the Master was on day nine and had 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep in the Master's fatigue diary. No relief master is rostered. The roster could reach this occurrence only through fatigue, and the evidence discussed below gives no sign of it on the night. It is unlikely that the roster influenced the occurrence. It is likely that it increased risk, because the exposure recurs on every darkness transit, with a fatigue diary the operator asks for and does not collect.

The plotter fault passed on verbally at the handover also increased risk without influencing the occurrence. The outgoing master told the Master of both morning freezes at about 13:05 at the town wharf, which is what OPS-9 9.3 required. The Master replied that it had done the same a month before, and neither made an entry. The freeze at 18:07 was a firmware fault. An entry at 13:05 would have been reviewed at the end of the week, and nothing written that afternoon could have applied firmware to the unit or taken the vessel off TF18 by 18:07. It is unlikely that this instance influenced the occurrence. It is likely that it increased risk, because both masters described the same practice, and a fault passed on by word of mouth leaves the next master knowing and everyone ashore not. The defect chain that does reach the freeze runs through the procedure described above.

The forward saloon lifejacket locker is a further factor of this kind. The vessel carried 40 adult jackets in a locker behind the kiosk counter in the forward saloon. The 2011 approved arrangement had an open bench in that position, and the counter was fitted in a 2019 refit under a minor modification notice that did not trigger a re-survey. The survey on 16/07/2026 found that the locker face cannot be reached from 22 of the 34 forward saloon seats without passing behind the counter through a 0.6 m gap. The muster placard directs passengers to a locker they cannot see from their seats. The Deckhand had to ask three passengers at the counter to move and hand jackets out over it. The operator says the same counter is fitted to its two other 24 m vessels. All 38 passengers were in lifejackets by about 18:22 and ashore by 19:26. The vessel was upright, stable and not sinking, so it is unlikely that the locker influenced the grounding or its outcome. It is very likely that the arrangement increased risk to the people in the saloon, because a fire, a capsize risk or an injured crew member would leave passengers unable to equip themselves. Matters examined and not settled

Boat ramp floodlights

The foreshore survey of 18/07/2026 found 14 unshielded LED floodlights on 12 m columns at the new boat ramp, commissioned on 22/05/2026, ten days before the winter timetable began. Each presented about 4,800 candela toward the channel. From 0.5 nm north of the beacon the array lay behind it within 4 degrees of the same bearing and 1.5 degrees of the same elevation. It was continuously lit, while the beacon flashed green for 0.4 seconds every 2.5 seconds. The Council's planning unit approved the redevelopment, and the Port Authority's aids to navigation officer was not consulted.

The Master described looking "into a wall of light" and said that in front of it the beacon was "a nothing". The outgoing master independently described the beacon as washed out from up the top since the car park lighting went in. For at least the last 37 seconds before the Master called the beacon it was clear of the islet and not seen, and in those seconds the floodlights, and not the canopy, lay behind the beacon.

Against this, the canopy screened the beacon over most of the search, so it would not have been visible against a black background either. The heading change began before the search, so the floodlights cannot have caused the turn. The only measurement was a survey eleven days later, and nothing gives a detection threshold for a 0.4 second green flash against that background. The Master said twice that they could not tell whether the lights were why the beacon could not be seen. The evidence is evenly balanced on whether the floodlights delayed the sighting, and so the moment the held heading was noticed. The question could not be resolved because nothing was measured on the night. [NOT ESTABLISHED: a detection threshold for a 0.4 second green flash against the floodlight background, or a night trial under comparable conditions]

Fatigue

The Master was on day nine of a twelve-day tour, and the channel transit fell in the last hour and a quarter of a 13 hour 40 minute spread. The Master's diary gave 6 hours 15 minutes of sleep the night before, and in interview the Master said: "I was tired. I'd be lying if I said otherwise." Easing the vessel back to port when it was nearly 40 m west of the centreline, believing it just outside the edge, is the kind of misjudgement fatigue is expected to produce.

Against this, the Master also said "I wasn't fighting to stay awake and I wasn't slow", and the recorded performance agreed. Helm work held the centreline to within 3 m for the first two minutes in the channel. The response to the shallow alarm took four seconds, the radio work after the grounding was complete at the first attempt, and the decision not to refloat took about thirty seconds. The Master said 6 hours 15 minutes was normal on a split. Whether the Master was fatigued cannot be determined either way. No detailed fatigue assessment was made, and every decision that mattered on the night is either answered by another factor or contradicted by the recorded data, so a finding of fatigue would not alter the chain. [NOT ESTABLISHED: a detailed fatigue assessment of the Master]

Hypotheses examined and not supported

Two hypotheses were examined and not supported. A tide set down below prediction over Boolarong Bank was very unlikely. The Port Authority gauge read 0.91 m at 18:12 against a predicted 0.94 m, and the gauge's largest departure from the table in the twelve hours to 20:00 was 0.07 m. With the bed at 0.50 m below chart datum there was 1.41 m of water against a static draught of 1.35 m plus 0.18 m of squat at 6.8 kt. At the predicted height there would have been 1.44 m against an effective draught of 1.53 m, so the vessel would have touched at the predicted tide as well.

A steering or propulsion failure before the vessel left the centreline was also very unlikely. Both engines held 1,780 and 1,784 rpm, within 12 rpm of each other, from 18:03 to 18:11:52 with no alarm. Steering hydraulic pressure held at 96 to 99 bar against a normal band of 90 to 105 bar. Rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees, and the rate of turn returned to zero, which shows a heading applied and held and not a sheer. The steering system was removed and tested on 12/07/2026 and every component was serviceable. The starboard shaft, propeller and rudder damage dated from the contact.

What worked

The Master's actions after the grounding limited the consequences. Both engines were stopped 27 seconds after contact and were not restarted, and the pan pan at 18:13:04 stated "I am not attempting to refloat" as a decision already made. The Master's reasoning in interview was a falling tide, an unknown bottom, 38 people aboard and nine seconds of grinding, and the Master said "On the bank she can't sink." The hull was holed with a 180 mm split in the plating in way of the No. 2 starboard void. The Master had the void sounded, reported about 75 mm of ingress at 18:17:05 and had it sounded every ten minutes. The ingress reached about 260 mm by the time the vessel refloated at 00:20. Backing off a holed vessel into the channel on a falling tide at night would have put a flooding compartment into deep water with the passengers aboard. It is very likely that the decision not to refloat reduced risk. The first pan pan gave the position, persons on board, injuries and pollution at the first attempt, and the passengers were addressed within 36 seconds of the impact and again at 18:14:52. The workboat came alongside at 18:41 and the last passenger was ashore at 19:26. Both masters also disclosed the missing defect entry without being asked.

Safety actions

Work order WO-176 was funded from the 2026 waterways contingency and the Merrandi Islet canopy was trimmed to 2 m on 24/07/2026, restoring the No. 4 beacon's sightline over the northern approach. A three-yearly trimming cycle has been programmed, and the sightline is to be re-measured from the inbound track on completion. The Aids to Navigation Officer, Kanooka Shire Council, issued local notice LNM-2026-14 on 22/07/2026 giving the solar conversion and the 3 M nominal range. The Port Authority's aids to navigation register was made available to every commercial operator using the channel, and Tarrakin Ferries has reissued the passage plan appendix as issue 3 with the corrected range. The notice and the reissue are recorded as in progress.

Two recommendations are open, each with a response due on 30/09/2026: that the aids to navigation services agreement replace the 50 m vegetation scope at schedule 2.4 with a sightline test, and that Tarrakin Ferries write a night passage plan for the Merrandi Channel before any further darkness transit and name a hold point, so that the loss of the primary means of position fixing inside the channel requires the way to be taken off the vessel until the position is re-established by another means. [NOT ESTABLISHED: outcome of the open recommendations after the 30/09/2026 response date]

Findings summary

The standard of proof applied in this investigation was "Likely or probable".

Contributing factors

  1. It is virtually certain that clearing of the mangrove canopy that screened the No. 4 beacon was deferred unfunded at the 2023, 2024 and 2025 works rounds, and this very likely contributed to the grounding because it left the beacon screened from the channel. (Safety Issue)
  2. It is virtually certain that the last service, TF18, was moved into darkness from 01/06/2026 without reopening the daylight-only route risk assessment for the Merrandi Channel, and this likely contributed to the grounding because no night passage plan was then written. (Safety Issue)
  3. It is virtually certain that there was no night passage plan and no hold point for loss of the primary means of position fixing, and this very likely contributed to the grounding because the transit continued at eight knots after the chart plotter froze. (Safety Issue)
  4. It is virtually certain that the operator's defect procedure never required a fault that had cleared itself to be recorded, and this likely contributed to the grounding because earlier plotter freezes were never written down and the firmware fix was never applied. (Safety Issue)
  5. It is virtually certain that the No. 4 beacon was screened by mangroves from the channel between 0.84 nm and 0.34 nm north of it, and this likely contributed to the grounding because the one reference that would have shown the new heading was not visible.
  6. It is virtually certain that the chart plotter display froze during the channel transit and did not recover, and this very likely contributed to the grounding because the master then had no position fix of any kind for the rest of the transit.
  7. It is virtually certain that the master eased the heading five degrees to starboard without a decision to turn, and it is virtually certain that this took the vessel out of the dredged channel.
  8. It is virtually certain that the transit continued at eight knots from the plotter freeze until the shallow alarm, and this very likely contributed to the grounding because the vessel could have been stopped in the channel at any time up to the western edge and after the beacon was sighted.
  9. It is virtually certain that the vessel left the dredged channel on the bank side, and it is virtually certain that the grounding followed directly from this.
  10. It is virtually certain that the shallow alarm was set at its 2019 commissioning value of 0.9 m under the keel, and this very likely contributed to the grounding because the 16 seconds of warning it gave were less than the vessel needed for a crash stop.

Other factors that increased risk

  1. It is virtually certain that the Waterways Aids to Navigation Code placed no availability or notice duty on beacons off declared shipping channels, and it is unlikely that this contributed to the grounding, but it likely increased risk because users of the Merrandi Channel are not told of changes to its aids. (Safety Issue)
  2. It is virtually certain that the No. 4 beacon's nominal range was halved from 6 to 3 nautical miles by a solar conversion in 11/2025 with no notice to channel users, and it is unlikely that this contributed to the grounding, but it likely increased risk because the operator's passage plan still described a 6 M light. (Safety Issue)
  3. It is virtually certain that the winter roster placed the darkness transit at the close of a split duty that ended 20 minutes inside the operator's spread limit, and it is unlikely that this contributed to the grounding, but it likely increased risk because the exposure recurs on every darkness transit of the timetable. (Safety Issue)
  4. It is virtually certain that the plotter's two morning freezes were passed on verbally at the change of master and not entered in the defect book, and it is unlikely that this contributed to the grounding because no entry made that afternoon could have corrected the firmware fault by the time of the freeze, but it likely increased risk because both masters followed the same practice.
  5. It is virtually certain that the forward saloon lifejacket locker was blocked by a kiosk counter fitted in a 2019 refit without a re-survey of the safety equipment arrangement, and on the tests recorded so far it is unlikely that this contributed to the grounding, but it is very likely that it increased risk because passengers could not reach the locker without crew help. (Safety Issue)

Other findings

  1. It is virtually certain that both engines were stopped after contact and that no attempt was made to refloat the vessel on a falling tide, and this very likely decreased risk because the vessel was holed in the compartment it was resting on and was not moved into deep water with the passengers aboard.
  2. A tide set down below prediction over Boolarong Bank was considered and was very unlikely, because the gauge read 0.03 m below the tide table at the time of the grounding and the vessel would have touched at the predicted height as well.
  3. A steering or propulsion failure before the vessel left the centreline was considered and was very unlikely, because the recorded engine, steering pressure and rudder data showed no fault and the removed steering components were all serviceable.
  4. It is virtually certain that unshielded boat ramp floodlights lay behind the No. 4 beacon from the north, but whether they delayed the sighting of the beacon was about as likely as not, so no finding is made on their contribution.
  5. Whether the master was fatigued during the channel transit was about as likely as not, so no finding is made on fatigue.

Appendix B: Excluded hypotheses

Two hypotheses were tested and not supported. Each was very unlikely to have existed, and each is set out with the measurements that bore on it.

Tide set down below prediction over Boolarong Bank (very unlikely). The hypothesis was tested because the vessel grounded three hours into a falling tide with a two-day westerly behind it, when a set-down of a few tenths of a metre would have mattered. The Port Authority's gauge at Kanooka Heads read 0.91 m at 18:12 against a predicted 0.94 m, so the stand was 0.03 m under the tide table. The gauge's largest departure from the table in the twelve hours to 20:00 was 0.07 m. The bed at the contact point was surveyed at 0.50 m below chart datum, which gave 1.41 m of water against a static draught of 1.35 m and a calculated squat of 0.18 m at 6.8 kt. At the predicted height there would have been 1.44 m of water against an effective draught of 1.53 m, so the vessel would have touched at the predicted tide as well. The vessel touched because it was 54 m outside a channel dredged to 3.2 m.

Steering or propulsion failure before the vessel left the centreline (very unlikely). The hypothesis was tested because a five degree heading change followed by a steady set out of the channel can look like a jammed rudder or a lost engine. Three findings did not support it.

  • The engine recorder gave both engines at 1,780 and 1,784 rpm, within 12 rpm of each other, from 18:03 to 18:11:52, with no alarm, no excursion and no throttle movement.
  • Steering gear hydraulic pressure held at 96 to 99 bar against a normal band of 90 to 105 bar, and rudder angle followed helm demand within 1.5 degrees throughout.
  • The rate of turn peaked at 6 degrees per minute and returned to zero, which is a heading applied and then held rather than a sheer.

The whole steering system was removed and function tested on 12/07/2026. Every component was serviceable, with no internal leakage and no sign of a pre-existing defect. The starboard shaft, propeller and rudder damage dated from the contact, and the bridge audio contains no steering or engine remark at any point.
